title: Matthew 3:7–12
context: John confronts Pharisees and Sadducees seeking baptism without fruit: viper brood, Abrahamic presumption, axe at the root, and a Coming One who baptizes with Spirit and fire and separates wheat from chaff.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: On repentance, wrath, and fruit, a few classic voices from each tradition.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: The grace or love of God, whence cometh our salvation, is FREE IN ALL, and FREE FOR ALL.

I ascribe to grace the commencement, the continuance and the consummation of all good… I believe, according to the scriptures, that many persons resist the Holy Spirit and reject the grace that is offered.

reformed.quote: We call predestination God’s eternal decree, by which he determined with himself what he willed to become of each man. For all are not created in equal condition; rather, eternal life is foreordained for some, eternal damnation for others.

But now that election operates according to grace, there is hope even for the most wretched. If work and reward were the standard of admission into the kingdom of heaven, its gates would be opened for no one.

verses.text: But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming for his baptism, he said to them, “You offspring of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
verses.arminianNotes:
Religious leaders arrive, and John does not flatter them. “Offspring of vipers” and “wrath to come” strip pedigree of safety. Fleeing wrath is wise only if fruit follows.

The warning is sincere. Wrath is in earnest, and hearers are summoned to flee it by true repentance—not by a baptism that leaves the heart unchanged.
verses.reformedNotes:
John exposes counterfeit approach to baptism. Wrath is coming; religious labels do not cancel it.

God’s judgment is not a scare tactic without substance. The prophet’s harshness is mercy that tells the truth before the axe falls.

verses.text: Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance!
verses.arminianNotes:
Repentance has a matching harvest. Fruit in keeping with means a life that fits the turn claimed at the water.

Arminians preach this as moral change under grace. Confession without fruit is incomplete; grace enables a new walk that can and should appear.
verses.reformedNotes:
Fruit authenticates repentance. John refuses empty profession.

New life shows. Fruit is evidence of a heart God has turned—not a wage that buys pardon, yet never optional window dressing.
verses.keyContrast: Both demand fruit with repentance. Arminians underline grace-enabled responsibility to produce a matching life; Calvinists emphasize fruit as necessary evidence of a repentance God has wrought.

verses.text: Don’t think to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham for our father,’ for I tell you that God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones.
verses.arminianNotes:
Abrahamic descent is no shelter from wrath. God can raise children from stones—heritage cannot replace faith and fruit.

Privilege without response is presumption. The invitation remains open, but ancestry does not save.
verses.reformedNotes:
Covenant privilege without faith is empty. God is free to create a people for Abraham beyond bloodlines.

Election and promise are God’s to fulfill. Stones-language humbles every boast in flesh while magnifying God’s power to raise a true seed.

verses.text: Even now the ax lies at the root of the trees. Therefore every tree that doesn’t produce good fruit is cut down, and cast into the fire.
verses.arminianNotes:
The axe is already at the root—judgment is near, not theoretical. Fruitless trees face fire.

Repent while the axe has not yet swung. The warning aims at conversion, not despair alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Even now” marks present crisis. Fruitless trees are cut down and burned.

Final judgment is rooted in God’s righteousness. The axe image is gospel seriousness that drives sinners to the Coming One, not to self-repair.

verses.text: “I indeed baptize you in water for repentance, but he who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit.
verses.arminianNotes:
John’s water baptism is for repentance; the Coming One is mightier and baptizes with Spirit and fire. John decreases; Jesus surpasses.

The Spirit’s work is offered in the Mightier One. Fire can purify or judge; either way, Jesus’ baptism eclipses John’s.
verses.reformedNotes:
John’s humility frames Jesus’ supremacy. Spirit-and-fire baptism is the Messiah’s own work.

The Spirit is given by the Son according to the Father’s purpose. John’s ministry is preparatory; Christ’s is decisive and effectual.

verses.text: His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor. He will gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn up with unquenchable fire.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Winnowing separates wheat and chaff. Jesus gathers and burns; the invitation to be wheat is urgent under unquenchable fire.

Flee chaff’s end by true repentance and faith in the Coming One. The fork is in His hand—respond while gathering is still offered.
verses.reformedNotes:
The threshing floor is His; wheat and chaff meet different ends. Gathering and burning are the Messiah’s acts.

Christ clears His floor completely. Judgment and salvation are not left unfinished; the barn and the fire both display His lordship.
verses.keyContrast: Both preach separation under Christ. Arminians typically stress the sincere call to repent and become wheat; Reformed commentators stress Christ’s effectual clearing of His floor—gathering His wheat and judging the chaff.
